title: Ellefson v. Megadeth, Inc. — assigned problem, source-limited
citation: 2005 WL 82022 (S.D.N.Y. 2005), as cited in the assigned problem
lead: A settlement’s text arrives before a deadline but its signature arrives afterward; subsequent execution, mailing and attempted withdrawal create a formation question whose judicial answer is missing from the assignment.

actors.role: Megadeth member bringing a profit-distribution fraud suit.

limits: The complete judicial opinion remains unrecovered. The chronology is the assignment’s account, not independently verified judicial findings. Contract conditions, choice of law, signature details, author, final order and subsequent history remain unresolved.

sections.title: A profit dispute moves into settlement negotiations
sections.cue: What deadline did the defendants announce?
paragraphs: Ellefson, a member of Megadeth, sued the band for fraud arising from a disagreement over profit distribution. The parties’ lawyers negotiated a Settlement and General Release, revising it repeatedly over several weeks.

On May 13, 2004, the defendants emailed that they would terminate the deal at 5 p.m. Pacific time on May 14 unless they had a signed agreement in hand. The assignment makes that receipt deadline the starting point for the later formation questions.

sections.title: The completed text and the signature arrive on different sides of the deadline
sections.cue: What was sent at each time?
paragraphs: The agreement was finalized and sent to the defendants at 4:45 p.m. on May 14. Ellefson’s signature page was not faxed until 5:16 p.m., after the stated deadline.

Sending the text before 5 p.m. and sending the signature afterward were separate events. The chronology therefore does not simply show timely receipt of the signed agreement the defendants had requested.

sources.pinpoint: Text and signature timing; assigned printed 268

sections.title: Execution and mailing precede an attempted withdrawal
sections.cue: Why did the dispute continue beyond the late signature?
paragraphs: On May 20, defense counsel sent fully executed copies to all parties by regular mail. On May 24, Ellefson’s lawyer purported to withdraw from negotiations. Defense counsel answered that a signed agreement already existed. Ellefson received the copies mailed May 20 on June 2.
The defendants moved to enforce the settlement. Their later execution and mailing, and the timing of the attempted withdrawal, raised questions beyond whether the first deadline had been missed.

sources.pinpoint: Mailing, withdrawal and motion; assigned printed 268

sections.title: The assigned problem stops at the enforcement question
paragraphs: The textbook asks whether the court should grant enforcement and points to its discussion of tardy acceptances. The sequence requires attention to the receipt deadline, the late signature, possible acceptance through later conduct, and whether withdrawal preceded a legally effective agreement.

The assignment does not give the court’s answer or full reasoning. It does not identify which defendant signed when, reproduce every contractual condition or establish a choice-of-law ruling. Without the actual decision, no enforcement order, dismissal, fee award or appellate outcome can be supplied as the result of this case.
